newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe revises Zimbabwe's 1996 GDP growth rate up.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe revises Zimbabwe's 1996 GDP growth rate up.

text.p: President Robert Mugabe said on Thursday Zimbabwe's agriculture-based economy will grow eight percent in 1996, higher than previous projections.

In an end-of-the-year address to parliament, Mugabe said the rise was based on a 49 percent growth in the key farming sector, which fell 12 percent in 1995, and on generally high commodity prices during 1996. Agriculture makes up about 15 percent of Zimbabwe's GDP.

"The economic upturn has stimulated renewed confidence within the agricultural industry and the economy as a whole. As a result, the economy is expected to register a gross domestic product growth (GDP) rate of eight percent in 1996," he said.
The growth figure was one percentage point above the previous official forecast and three percentage points above independent estimates.
Mugabe said the manufacturing sector was expected to grow by 3.2 percent in 1996 compared to declining 14.2 percent in 1995.
But mine production, he said, was expected to decline 1.1 percent in volume in 1996 compared to 10.5 percent growth in 1995.

"This downward trend, attributable to reduced international demand for base metals, is anticipated to be reversed in the coming year due to the combined effect of increased local production and firm international metal prices," he said.
Mugabe added the sector would also benefit from increased exploration, particularly for gold, diamonds, copper and zinc.

He gave no projection for next year, but finance officials and some Zimbabwean economists see GDP growth at between five and seven percent because of predictions the current farming season will have near-normal rains.

Mugabe told parliament his government would make vigorous efforts to support sustainable development in the agriculture sector, including using donor funds to improve infrastructure, suchs as roads, dams and irrigation schemes.

He said the government would soon detail an agricultural sector investment programme extending to the year 2020 as part of the drive to reduce poverty and unemployment, estimated in 1996 by many economists at between 40 and 50 percent.
